analysis.one_liner: Expands federal workplace safety law to government employees, strengthens whistleblower protections, and raises fines and prison terms for employers whose violations kill or injure workers.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 24 senators backing it, was referred to the Senate labor committee in August 2009 and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 does not cover federal, state, and local government employees, and its penalties are small — the top fine for a violation that kills a worker is $70,000. This bill would bring public employees under OSHA coverage, make it easier for workers to report injuries and refuse dangerous work without being fired, guarantee paid time for workers who help with inspections, and give injured workers and their families a formal role when the government investigates. It also raises fines to as much as $250,000 when a violation kills a worker, adds up to 10 years in prison for a willful violation that causes death, and holds corporate officers personally responsible.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 8 million public employees not covered by federal safety law would gain OSHA protections. Workers in covered private workplaces would gain stronger whistleblower rights, protection from employer policies that discourage injury reporting, paid time for inspections, and formal rights when they or a family member are hurt on the job. Employers with good safety records face little change; violators face sharply higher penalties.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public employees and workers at covered workplaces

how_it_helps.text: Amends the OSH Act's definition of employer to include the United States, states, and their political subdivisions, extending OSHA coverage to government employees who are currently excluded [S3].

Expands whistleblower protection to cover reporting injuries or unsafe conditions to employers or safety committees, and protects workers who refuse dangerous work when a reasonable person would see a bona fide risk of serious injury [S3].
Provides that time spent participating in or aiding a safety inspection is paid work time, and bars employers from any loss of wages or benefits for it [S3].
Requires employers to notify the Labor Department of any workplace death or incident hospitalizing two or more workers, and to preserve evidence for the investigation [S3].
Gives injured workers and families of killed workers the right to meet with investigators, receive copies of citations, and object before citations are withdrawn or modified in settlement [S3].

Raises civil penalties — up to $250,000 for a violation that kills a worker, adjusted for inflation every four years — and raises criminal penalties to up to 10 years in prison for a willful violation causing death and up to 5 years for one causing serious bodily injury, applying to responsible corporate officers personally [S3].
Bars employers from adopting policies that discourage workers from reporting work-related injuries or illnesses, and prohibits unclassified citations that mask the severity of violations [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers — private companies and federal, state, and local government agencies — bear the cost of compliance, injury-reporting rules, and inspections, and violators face dramatically higher fines and possible criminal prosecution of corporate officers. State-plan states must update their programs within 12 months; non-plan states and localities have up to 36 months [S3].

drawbacks.text: The cost falls partly on government employers, meaning state and local agencies — and ultimately taxpayers — would fund safety compliance and potentially higher penalties for their own operations [S3].

Raising the maximum penalty for a worker death to $250,000 and criminal exposure to 10 years imposes real costs on employers, and honest supporters would acknowledge that higher penalties can pressure smaller employers and may not by themselves improve safety outcomes without stronger enforcement capacity.

Employers would face a faster, less familiar whistleblower process, including a preliminary reinstatement order that takes effect before a hearing is complete, which critics would argue raises the risk of erroneous findings against them [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is worker safety and accountability against compliance and penalty costs for employers, including public agencies. The design includes offsets that soften the cost: the Labor Secretary can cede jurisdiction to other federal agencies with equally effective safety programs to avoid duplication, and mines stay under the Mine Safety and Health Act [S3]. Small employers (25 or fewer workers) get lower minimum penalties in fatality cases [S3]. On balance the bill's benefits to workers are large and its costs fall mainly on violators, but the burden on small government units in non-plan states is real and staggered only partially.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read the bill once, sent it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and it sat there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Kennedy introduced the bill on August 5, 2009, with Senator Reid introducing it on his behalf and 20 other Democratic senators as original cosponsors [S3].
Twenty-four senators cosponsored — 22 of the Senate's 58 Democrats, the Senate's sole Independent, and its sole Independent Democrat [S4].

The Senate referred the bill to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on August 5, 2009, and the action history shows no further action of any kind — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor consideration [S5].
The bill died in committee when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, never reaching a vote in either chamber [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Covered employers, particularly those relying on the low $70,000 maximum penalty and the exclusion of public employees from OSHA coverage, are better off because the bill never advanced; workers who would have gained expanded protections got nothing.

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to expand OSHA coverage, strengthen whistleblower protections, and raise penalties [S3].

for.name: Sen. Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on Kennedy's behalf [S3].

for.name: Senate's sole Independent and sole Independent Democrat
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making all cosponsors non-Republicans [S4].

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after its referral; no hearing, markup, or committee vote appears in the action history [S5].

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and employer associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed the Protecting America's Workers Act, citing sharply higher penalties and criminal liability for employers.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 24 cosponsors were Democrats, the Senate's Independent, or its Independent Democrat; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never reached a vote where the party split could be recorded.

industries.industry: Covered private employers (construction, manufacturing, and other OSHA-regulated industries)
industries.note: The bill multiplies their exposure: civil penalties up to $250,000 for a fatal violation, criminal sentences up to 10 years with personal liability for responsible corporate officers, and bans on policies discouraging injury reporting [S3]. Its interest in avoiding these costs runs against workers' interest in enforceable safety rules.

industries.industry: Federal, state, and local government employers
industries.note: Public agencies would come under OSHA coverage for the first time and bear compliance and penalty costs, but their employees are precisely the workers who gain protection [S3].

industries.industry: Workplace safety compliance and consulting services
industries.note: New posting, notification, and state-plan conformity requirements would create demand for safety compliance services as employers adjust to the new rules [S3].
